2026 Paris Motor Show • Hyundai Tucson N Line Steals the Spotlight in Paris, but It's All Show and No Go
1970 Buick GSX 455 in Saturn Yellow Is a Rare 4-Speed Luxury Muscle Car, Paint Job Took 17 Months
50 photos
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy
Imagine your family doctor showing up for a house call in 1970 driving a radioactive banana with a hood-mounted tachometer, black racing stripes, and a Hurst 4-speed stick shift. Wrap all that in a cloud of smoke, because 510 lb-ft of torque would tend to turn black rubber into white fog. Ask any Hemi owner from back then what was it like to look at that car from behind, and watch it pull away. That’s what the GSX was all about – elegant manners of a tire iron adorned with a silk pompon.
No, not GTX; one letter before that – T is right after S in the alphabet, and the GTX was behind the GSX on the drag strip. And in cubic inches. And in torque. And in swagger. That glorious contradiction is the exact vibe radiating from the 1970 Buick GSX 455 featured by automotive journalist Jim Campisano on his Muscle Car Campy YouTube channel, where owner Timothy Blanch shows off one of Flint’s loudest velvet-gloved street brawlers ever.
Blanch is a die-hard Bowtie loyalist who has owned his 1969 Chevrolet Camaro for 45 years and kept a Chevrolet Chevelle for 12 years before crossing into Buick territory. After 43 years of work, Tim Blanch retired, and found himself a new hobby – restoring the most luxurious muscle car ever made.
A friend pulled this GSX out of New England 15 years ago, and Blanch traded his Chevelle to acquire it in 2016. He stripped the car, shipped the shell to Pennsylvania for a 17-month paint job, and reassembled it himself. I don’t know what they did in that paint booth for almost a year and a half, but its looks could stop Saturn’s moons in their orbit, that’s how yellow it is. Saturn Yellow, to be precise. (and please note that Saturn has 293 confirmed natural satellites, but NASA’s still counting).
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Even after finishing the wrenching, Blanch waited a full year to score the proper reproduction wheels before letting Campisano film the ride. Wearing the blinding Saturn Yellow paint, identified by the exclusive QQ trim tag code that General Motors reserved solely for the 1970 GSX, this coupe radiates attitude. Inside, it skips air conditioning for a Sonoramic AM radio, a short consolette, and a padded GSX tilt wheel measuring one inch less in diameter than the regular Buick GS 455. “Regular.”
As both men point out while rowing the Muncie M20 wide-ratio 4-speed gearbox, the Buick cabin looks way more upscale and chrome-trimmed than any period Chevelle SS. That country-club swagger paired with street-brawler punch goes right back to the birth of the Gran Sport moniker. Buick launched the Skylark Gran Sport midway through the 1965 model year on the intermediate A-body platform to give Pontiac’s hot-selling GTO a proper migraine.
Because General Motors brass banned intermediate cars from carrying engines reserved for the full-size series (usually larger than 400 cubic inches), Buick pulled a cheeky corporate sleight of hand for 1965 and 1966. Engineers dropped in their venerable 401-cubic-inch Nailhead V8, slapped a Wildcat 445 sticker on the air cleaner, and called it a 400-incher.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy It churned out 325 horsepower at 4,400 rpm and a stump-pulling, tire-frying 445 pound-feet of torque at just 2,800 rpm. In 1967, Buick shortened the badge to GS 400 and retired the Nailhead for a modern 400-cubic-inch V8 rated at 340 horsepower and 440 pound-feet of torque, joined by a 260-horsepower GS 340 sibling.
A sleeker restyle in 1968 brought the 280-horsepower GS 350 alongside the GS 400, before the 455-cubic-inch behemoth arrived in 1970. The original rear-wheel-drive V8 Gran Sport bloodline finally bowed out after the 1975 model year.
When General Motors lifted its displacement cap for 1970, Buick unleashed the ultimate showroom magnet: the GSX, short for Gran Sport Experimental. Introduced in March 1970 to battle the Pontiac GTO Judge and Oldsmobile 4-4-2 W-30, the GSX package added chin and decklid spoilers, black stripes, front disc brakes, heavy-duty suspension, and wide tires. The $1,196 option, soon discounted to $1,100, stacked onto the $3,283 GS 455 hardtop base price.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy Under that black-striped hood lurked a lightweight 455-cubic-inch V8 that weighed roughly 150 pounds less than a Chrysler 426 Hemi or Chevrolet 454. Even in standard trim like Blanch’s car, with a 10.0:1 compression ratio and a four-barrel carburetor, the 455 delivered 350 horsepower at 4,600 rpm and an earth-spinning 510 pound-feet of torque at 2,800 rpm. That torque figure stood as an American production car record for 33 years.
Buyers who ticked the Stage 1 box got a 10.5:1 compression ratio, bigger valves, a wilder camshaft, and a reworked Rochester Quadrajet carburetor. Buick advertised it at 360 horsepower at 4,600 rpm and 510 pound-feet of torque to fool insurers, though real output topped 400 horsepower. Period testers clocked the base 455 GSX from 0 to 60 mph in 6.5 seconds, running the quarter-mile in 14.28 seconds at 100.5 mph.
With a top speed reaching 129 mph in Car Life testing, the big Buick had serious legs, while Motor Trend rocketed a 1970 Stage 1 from 0 to 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and through the quarter-mile in a blistering 13.38 seconds at 105.5 mph. Despite those superhero numbers, buyers were scarce across its three-year run from 1970 to 1972, with Buick assembling just 846 GSX coupes in total. There were no other body styles available, by the way.
Photo: YouTube/Muscle Car Campy The debut 1970 model year accounted for 678 of those cars, split by color into 491 Saturn Yellow examples and 187 Apollo White ones. By engine, 400 buyers upgraded to the Stage 1 455, while 278 kept the standard 350-horsepower 455. Across all 678 cars, 479 carried the optional Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 3-speed automatic transmission, leaving only 199 factory examples equipped with the 4-speed manual gearbox and Hurst floor shifter.
Digging deeper into 1970 records, those 400 Stage 1 cars included 118 4-speeds (78 yellow and 40 white) and 282 automatics (214 yellow and 68 white). Meanwhile, the 278 standard 455 coupes featured 197 automatics (142 yellow and 55 white) and just 81 4-speeds, split into 57 in Saturn Yellow like Blanch’s gem and 24 in Apollo White, though some archives tally 79 base manuals and 120 Stage 1 sticks.
By 1971, tightening emissions dropped compression to 8.5:1, trimming ratings to 315 horsepower and 450 pound-feet on the base 455, and 345 horsepower with 460 pound-feet on the Stage 1, while Buick also opened the GSX package to additional factory colors and the 260-horsepower 350-cubic-inch V8. Production tumbled to 124 cars for 1971, which enthusiast registries estimate at roughly 62 Stage 1s, 30 standard 455s, and 32 small-block 350 coupes.
In 1972, a switch to SAE net ratings adjusted the 455 to 250 horsepower and the Stage 1 to 270 horsepower, and only 44 final-year GSXs left the factory. Those 44 cars comprised 16 350-cubic-inch models (15 automatics, and a single 4-speed), 4 base 455s (3 automatics, 1 4-speed), and 24 Stage 1s (22 automatics, a pair of 4-speeds).
